title: Pay business bills before Dec 31? The cash-method rule
label: Year-end tax move

hook.sub: The timing rule for business bills.

lines: Rosa's software renewal is due in January.
She could pay it on Dec. 30.

beats.note: Prepaid for 12 months or less? It can usually count when paid.

items.t: Keep the receipt and the date paid
Don't buy just for the deduction

cta.sub: We'll DM you our year-end planning page.

captions.instagram:
Paying a business bill on Dec. 30 instead of Jan. 2 can move the deduction into 2026.

✔️ Most small businesses use the cash method: you generally deduct an expense in the year you actually pay it.
✔️ Paid in advance for years? It's generally spread over the years it covers.
✔️ The 12-month rule: a prepaid benefit that ends within 12 months (and by the end of next year) can usually count when paid.
✔️ Pay what the business needs anyway. A deduction lowers taxable income; it isn't a discount.

Our year-end planning page lists the moves that only count if done by Dec. 31.

captions.youtube_description: Under the cash method you generally deduct a business expense in the year you pay it, so a bill paid Dec. 30 counts for 2026 and the same bill paid Jan. 2 counts for 2027. Prepaid multi-year costs are spread out, except under the 12-month rule. Pay only what the business needs.

captions.pinterest_description: Year-end tax planning for small business owners: under the cash method, business expenses generally count in the year you pay them. A bill paid Dec. 30 counts for 2026; paid Jan. 2, it counts for 2027. Prepaid costs follow the 12-month rule. Keep receipts and buy only what the business needs.

sources.fact: Cash method: generally deduct expenses in the tax year you actually pay them; prepaid expenses deductible only in the year they apply to, except the 12-month rule (benefit ends by the earlier of 12 months after it begins or the end of the tax year after the payment year); read 2026-10-30
